title: Rejection of Fluorescence Background in Resonance and Spontaneous Raman Microspectroscopy
protocol: Place biological samples on a No. 1 thickness coverslip mounted in an Attofluor cell chamber.
Prepare liquid samples, particularly toxic ones, in a small glass bottle with a coverslip cemented to the opening by means of a silicone epoxy.
Invert the prepared bottle for measurement purposes.
Mount the sample on a secondary stage that has its own independent focus control.
Pass the light through a Faraday isolator.
Place a half-wave plate before the Faraday isolator for continuous tuning of total power.
Send the beam through a bandpass filter with 0.8 nm FWHM centered at 808 nm.
Focus the beam by an achromatic doublet (f = 100 mm) onto a β-Barium Borate crystal.
Place the BBO crystal precisely symmetric about the focus of the doublet.
Align the crystal axis of the BBO crystal to the polarization of the incoming beam.
Use a second half-wave plate after the Faraday isolator for adjusting light intensity independently.
Recollimate the wavelength-converted light using a second achromatic doublet (f = 500 mm).
Direct the recollimated beam into an inverted microscope (IX-71, Olympus) via two steering mirrors.
Place a mirror in the sample plane of the microscope to align the excitation beam with the optic axis.
Iteratively tune the steering mirrors while observing back-reflected laser beam on a CCD camera attached to the imaging port of the microscope.
Center the image on the microscope's field-of-view for beam alignment.
Adjust the objective along the z-axis until the focal spot is centered and defocused beam center remains unchanged during translation.
Place a sample in the sample plane and irradiate with laser light to observe Raman scattering.
Use a dichroic filter below the microscope objective to separate Raman scattered light from the excitation beam.
Direct the Raman scattered light to the side port of the microscope.
Remove any lenses within the path for collimated signal light emergence.
Shrink the signal beam using a 0.47x telescope constructed of two achromatic doublets (f1 = 75 mm, f2 = 35 mm).
Polarize the signal light with a Glan-Thompson polarizer oriented at 0° with respect to vertical in the lab frame.
Direct the polarized signal light to a dichroic mirror where it is recombined with the pump beam.
Magnify the pump pulse by 0.35x using a telescope constructed with two achromatic doublets (f1 = 35 mm, f2 = 100 mm).
Send the magnified pump beam into a delay line composed of a right angle prism placed on a linear translation stage.
Tune the delay line to ensure temporal overlap between the pump and signal pulses.
Pass the pump beam through a half-wave plate oriented at an appropriate angle for optimal polarization.
Polarize the adjusted pump beam with a polarizer oriented at 45° with respect to vertical in the lab frame.
Reflect the light off of two steering mirrors.
Use piezo-electric controls on one mirror to finely adjust the position of the pump beam.
Overlap the pump beam spatially with the signal beam at a near point by adjusting the first steering mirror.
Adjust the beams at a far point using the piezo mirror to ensure collinearity.
Combine the two beams completely.
Set up the Kerr gate and collection system to maximize the collected time-gated signal.
Pass the pump and signal beams through a dichroic filter with an OD of 6 at 404 nm.
Focus both beams by an achromatic doublet (f = 35 mm) into a 1 cm pathlength quartz cuvette containing carbon disulfide (CS2).
Recollimate the light by a second doublet with a focal length identical to the first.
Pass the beams through a Glan-Thompson analyzer on a rotating mount.
Pass the beams through absorption and interference filters that have an OD of 10 at 808 nm.
Focus the signal light by an achromatic doublet (f = 35 mm) into a 50 μm multimode optical fiber.
Mount the fiber in a stage allowing translation in x, y, and z directions.
Couple the fiber to a commercial imaging spectrograph with attached CCD camera.
Align the analyzer to 0° with a test sample of toluene in the sample plane.
Adjust x, y, and z controls of the fiber mount to optimize the collected Raman signal.
Place a mirror in the sample plane of the microscope.
Remove the 404 nm filter from the system.
Rotate the analyzer to 90°.
Send the retroreflected 404 nm beam into the spectrograph with intensity adjusted to avoid saturation of the camera.
With the pump beam off, rotate the analyzer to minimize transmitted 404 nm signal.
Turn on the pump beam and slowly tune the delay stage until transmission of 404 nm light increases.
Iteratively adjust the delay stage, piezo-electric mirror, and x, y, z controls of the fiber to maximize the signal.
Place a strong Raman scatterer like toluene on the sample stage.
Tweak final alignment by adjusting delay stage, piezo-electric mirror, and x, y, z controls to optimize Raman signal.
Set the analyzer to 0° with excitation beam on and pump beam off.
Take an "ungated" spectrum without time-gating system benefit.
Set the analyzer to 90° with excitation and pump beams still off.
Take a background spectrum representing stray light leakage.
Keep the analyzer at 90°, turn all beams on.
Take a "gated" spectrum representing Raman scattered light.
With analyzer at 90°, excitation beam off, and pump beam on.
Take a second background spectrum for residual 808 nm light contribution.
Acquire a spectrum with all lasers off for baseline dark signal level.
Break integration time into several frames to correct cosmic rays.
Dark correct all spectra by subtracting the "dark" spectrum.
Compare several frames constituting one acquisition on a pixel-by-pixel basis.
Replace any pixel value that falls outside of 2 median deviations from the median value for that pixel across all frames with the median value across all frames.
Average and smooth the cosmic ray corrected frames using a Savitzky-Golay filter.
Subtract the "excitation-only" and "pump-only" spectra from the measured gated spectrum to extract the "true" gated spectrum.
Background correct the gated and ungated spectra by subtracting a 5th-order polynomial determined using the method of Lieber and Mahadevan-Jansen.
